I saw this rather amusing post and it made me realize that basic winterization steps are not going to be known by most that haven't lived in a climate where freezing temperatures are the norm during winter. I knew a guy that moved to an area that actually has a winter season and his irrigation system froze causing pipes to burst. He was a capable guy, he simply didn't know it needed to be turned off and drained. Which leads me to point one:

  • Drain your irrigation system for winter. You'll probably want to do this before it starts to freeze. This is a good video explaining the process. The video doesn't cover this, but if you have any drip filters you'll want to open them to let them drain then replace them. You'll also want to leave any bleeder screws on your valves open. The basics of this process are the same but not all irrigation systems are set up the same. For example, my irrigation supply and drain valves are located outside a few feet underground which requires an irrigation key to operate while the example in the video has them located in the basement of the house.

  • There is a reason your thermostat probably only goes down to 50 degrees F, that reason is to prevent damage from the cold. If it was cold enough in that house (see link above) to freeze the water in the tank of the toilet to the point that the tank burst, I guarantee there is other damage such as pipes bursting which means cutting holes in walls to fix. TL;DR the broken toilet tank in that other post is the least of that homes problems. Point being, if you have a house in an area that freezes regularly during the winter don't turn the heat off if you leave your house for an extended period of time, turn it down to 50.

  • The only other reasons I can think of for the toilet tank explosion would be not paying the bills or not keeping your heating system in good repair. There really is no valid argument for not paying your bills especially if those bills keep your house warm. As for keeping heating systems in good repair I must admit I have no clue. A quick search tells me get it inspected yearly. If anyone has any input on this it would be greatly appreciated.

  • Not all will have this option, but some will. If you have a wood stove that you don't use make sure you have wood for it in a covered area to last at least a week. You might consider a wood stove as a useless relic from some primitive era that can't be matched by the great technology that we now possess, you're wrong. Those things can heat an entire house in the dead of winter to near sauna temperatures. You can also use it for cooking. If you have one you should have the wood to fuel it and know how to use it.
Let's Talk Basic Home Maintenance, Specifically For Homes In Cold Weather

I'm going to +1 on the wood/coal stove. Had one in my last house, and that thing kicked out so much heat, that if you started it up when it was over 20 degree fahrenheit out, you'd be opening windows. It also came in very handy the couple of times the normal furnace died. I miss it.

Also, if you have a private well, check it out and do maintenance on it in the fall. You don't want to be outside, knee deep in water, in below freezing temperatures, pulling pipes and redrilling wells. Trust me on this one.

Another good tip is if you have a pool in the backyard, when you go to close the pool for the winter, place some empty bottles in the filter trap. When the water freezes, it expands. Having the empty bottles there will give the water a place to expand into instead of cracking the plastic casing, which can cause leaks.
